blindSummary:
This country carries severe risk for trans visitors, with religious-extremist violence escalating since the August 2024 political crisis that toppled the long-ruling government. A prominent trans activist was murdered at her home in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having "skyrocketed." Religious-fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been "forced into hiding." A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (one survivor said "I escaped only with my life").

Police extort third-gender and trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at the capital's international airport.

A foreign government's travel advisory places this country at its third warning level ("reconsider travel").
blindOutOfScope: Political instability, mob violence/lynchings, terrorism, and severe storms and seasonal flooding affect all travellers; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: LGBT-rights news site (Feb 2025): a prominent trans activist was brutally murdered in her home on 3 February 2025; police suspect extremists due to the nature of the attack. She was known for advocating legal recognition, healthcare access and safe spaces. An expatriate human-rights organisation of this country, based abroad, condemned the murder and called for legal reform.

LGBT-rights news site (April 2026): the expatriate organisation's annual report on 2025 documented 260 incidents of human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals in this country - a sharp increase continuing an upward trend since 2022 - including murder, arson and blackmail, with the interim government failing to protect them. A colonial-era penal-law provision criminalises same-sex relations; the 2013 third-gender recognition policy has not translated into effective protection or equal access to employment, healthcare, justice or services.

International journalism outlet feature: after the 2024 political upheaval, rising conservative religious influence has upended trans and third-gender lives in the capital - a mob stormed a third-gender safe house, community leaders went into hiding, and trans people are retreating from public life and erasing identities they once displayed openly. Notes third-gender recognition since 2013 and a trans woman elected mayor of a rural town in 2021.

NOTE: page content did not load at fetch time (only an LGBT news outlet's site navigation was retrieved); the underlying August 2025 article reports LGBTQ people in this country becoming increasingly vulnerable a year after the government was toppled.

A foreign home ministry's country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity in this country (updated April 2026): official asylum guidance assessing the legal position (the colonial-era penal provision), third-gender recognition, societal treatment, state protection levels, and risk to LGBT individuals - detailed country-of-origin information.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): an 1860 colonial-era penal code criminalises same-sex acts with up to life imprisonment; rarely enforced but used by police as a pretext to harass perceived LGBTIQ people. Members of the traditional third-gender community have been legally recognised as a third gender since 2014. Religious-fundamentalist groups have become vocal opponents - a professor at a national university publicly tore up a school textbook containing a transgender character, sparking backlash against gender diversity.

LGBT-rights news site (Oct 2025): dozens of third-gender people were arbitrarily arrested across the country after refusing to pay extortion money to police, per the expatriate organisation. In the main port city, at least twelve were injured in an assault after filing a police complaint; in a river-side industrial city, twelve were arrested while collecting money from vehicles - a traditional livelihood. The organisation alleges false extortion cases.

LGBT-rights news site (April 2024): five trans/third-gender women were arrested while begging near the capital's international airport and sentenced to one month by a mobile court for 'extortion' and 'public disturbance'. The expatriate organisation condemned the convictions as exacerbating the marginalisation of an already vulnerable group.

A foreign upper immigration tribunal's decision (Feb 2019): the asylum appeal of a gay man from this country - that country's home ministry accepted that the penal law criminalises same-sex activity but argued it is not fully enforced; the decision examines country evidence on the risk to gay men here - a detailed case-law assessment of the actual risk profile.
blindLocalsOnly: The traditional third-gender community is legally recognised as a third gender (2013/2014, a genuine positive), but there is no anti-discrimination law and no comprehensive legal gender recognition — resident-facing framework.
blindTangential: Same-sex conduct is criminalised under a colonial-era penal-code provision (life imprisonment, "rarely enforced" but used by police for harassment and extortion) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
